title: Not my worth
carry: what was lost was held, not who you are
last: I SAW WHAT YOU DID, AND IT MATTERED.

cards: The badge stops working at the door. Or the shop that was going to last forever puts a sign in the window. Or the body says no more to the job it did for years.
However it comes, losing work can feel like losing a name. Someone asks what you do, and for a while there's no easy answer. Today: Epictetus.

teach.h: A JOB FUSED WITH A SELF.
teach.b: First, the confusion. A job gives us a schedule, colleagues, a title, a paycheck and a ready answer at parties. It's easy to fuse all of that into a sense of who we are.
When the job goes, it can seem as if we've gone with it. Second, a Stoic teacher. Epictetus taught philosophy in the Roman world.
His handbook opens with a sorting: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Not in our power: our body, our property, our reputation, our offices, the positions we hold.

In our power: how we judge, what we aim for, what we turn away from. For Epictetus, a person's worth lives on that inside list. A job is on the outside list: given and taken, never the measure of a person.
Third, a man who lost everything. In the book of Job, in the Hebrew Bible, Job loses his wealth, his household, his children, all in one day.

teach.h: THE LORD GAVE, AND HATH TAKEN.
teach.b: And he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

teach.h: IT HURTS, AND IT'S NOT YOUR WORTH.
teach.b: Later in the book he argues, mourns and protests at length, and the text lets him. Some readers hear a distinction in that first line: what was given can be taken, and the one it was given to is still there.
Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a claim that losing work doesn't hurt.
Rent and purpose matter. Grief is fair, and Job is given room for it. Epictetus would ask for a cooler sorting.
What the two share is a narrower line: what was lost was held, not who you are, and the person who held it is still there.

how: People facing job loss often lean on community, faith or philosophy to keep their sense of worth apart from their work; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's sorting of what is and isn't in our power, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job.

o: a Greek god of work, wealth and good fortune
a Roman emperor who wrote about his own duties
a Stoic teacher who put jobs outside our power

games.q: who said what about losing — tap the pairs.
p: some things are in our power, some not
the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken

s: for Epictetus, the positions we hold are in our power
he lists offices with body, property and reputation among the things not in our power.
the book of Job lets Job argue, mourn and protest after his losses
the text gives his protest room; the first line is not the whole story.
saying a job isn't your worth means losing it shouldn't hurt
rent, purpose and grief are real; the claim is only that worth wasn't what was lost.

games.q: you're Epictetus, sorting the world into what's in our power and what isn't. where does a person's job title go?
games.why: he lists offices, the positions we hold, with body, property and reputation: not in our power. what is in our power is how we judge and what we aim for.

practice: Picture two baskets, and into the outer one gently set the things that can be given and taken: a title, a desk, a salary, how others see you.
Then notice what's left in you: how you pay attention, what you care about, how you meet this day. That's the inner basket; rest there.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus. The Stoic teacher who sorted the world into what's in our power and what isn't, and put a job on the outside list. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what was lost was held, not who you are. It hurts; it isn't your worth. See you tomorrow.
